query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal aging treatment that induces in situ surface segregation of Pt from the near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst will form a thin Pt‐rich surface layer. This engineered surface layer is expected to promote low‐temperature oxidation activity while conferring enhanced resistance to H2O and NO poisoning and improved long‐term durability without increasing the overall platinum‐group-metal loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst containing a low (trace) amount of Pt uniformly distributed throughout the bulk.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermal aging treatment under controlled oxidizing conditions (e.g., air or an inert gas with controlled water vapor) at a temperature selected to drive Pt segregation to the surface—without inducing significant sintering.
generation.conditions: The thermal aging is conducted at temperatures high enough to promote surface segregation (but below the sintering threshold) and is followed by performance evaluation under simulated automotive exhaust conditions. These include transient, low‐temperature operation (e.g., around 150 °C with periodic temperature spikes), exposure to water vapor and NO, and accelerated aging protocols that mimic vehicle lifetime operation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a Pt‐rich surface layer (or isolated single‐atom Pt sites) resulting from the thermal treatment.
generation.mechanism: Upon thermal aging, the high‐entropy alloy environment facilitates selective migration of Pt to the catalyst surface. The resulting Pt-rich surface sites lower the activation energy for oxidation reactions (improving low-temperature activity) and are less prone to poisoning due to their isolated nature. Meanwhile, the high-entropy bulk helps stabilize the overall structure against sintering and degradation over long-term operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the treated catalyst is predicted to exhibit a lower ignition temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation, enhanced resistance to deactivation by H2O and NO, and a smaller performance decline over extended aging. No increase in the overall platinum-group-metal content is required.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst, which displays suboptimal low-temperature activity, is more vulnerable to poisoning by moisture and NO, and degrades more rapidly over time.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected to manifest under automotive exhaust conditions that include transient and low-temperature operation with water vapor and NO present, as well as during accelerated aging tests representative of a vehicle’s lifetime exposure.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thermal aging temperature, duration, and oxidizing environment needed to achieve the optimal degree of Pt surface segregation and the exact magnitudes of improvement in catalytic activity and durability require experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts that are identical except that one set undergoes the controlled thermal aging treatment while the other remains unmodified. Subject both sets to simulated automotive exhaust testing including low temperatures, moisture, and NO exposure. Use surface-sensitive techniques (e.g., XPS, HAADF-STEM) to verify the formation of a Pt-rich surface layer on the treated samples.
measurements: Low-temperature oxidation ignition temperature (e.g., T10 or T50 for CO/hydrocarbon conversion)
Conversion rates in the presence of H2O and NO
Surface composition and Pt distribution (via XPS, STEM)
Durability/deactivation rates during prolonged aging tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged catalyst does not show a statistically significant decrease in the ignition temperature, improved resistance to H2O and NO poisoning, and evidence of Pt surface enrichment compared to the unmodified catalyst, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The catalytic oxidation of CO is a key heterogeneous gas‐solid process and a valuable probe for studying catalyst structure, metal‒support interactions, adsorption‐desorption behavior, and reaction mechanisms.[  ] The catalytic activity, stability, and water tolerance of the Pt/HEO for CO oxidation were systematically evaluated. As shown in Figure 4a, the Pt/HEO catalyst achieved full CO conversion at 195 °C, significantly lower than the 430 °C required by HEO nanofibers alone (Figure S33, Supporting Information), highlighting the critical role of Pt nanoparticles. cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation. Here we report high-entropy alloyed single-atom Pt (denoted hereafter as HEASA-Pt), which behaves as an active MOR catalyst without suffering from CO poisoning. Our design combines the high activity of the HEA structure and anti-CO poisoning capability resulting from the single-atom Pt sites in the alloy lattice. The designed HEASA-Pt, Pt1-NiCoMgBiSn, exhibits a notable mass activity of 35.3 A mg–1 (at 2.3 at% Pt), which is much higher than the activities of other MOR catalysts and commercial SA-Pt on carbon substrates (SA-Pt@C). Such high activity originates from the synergistic effect of multi-element coordination at each single-atom Pt site in Pt1-NiCoMgBiSn. The HEASA-Pt catalyst maintains high mass activity even after operation for 180,000 s, demonstrating good durability. In-situ Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and CO stripping tests reveal the good anti-CO poisoning capability of HEASA-Pt.
